newsitem.title: JAPAN: Tokyo stock market's five-day winning streak ends.
newsitem.headline: Tokyo stock market's five-day winning streak ends.

text.p: Tokyo stocks ended slightly lower on Tuesday after early gains brought on by a rebound in financial sector shares were eroded in the afternoon session, brokers said. They said the losses were expected as the Nikkei average had risen continuously in the past five sessions.
The 225-share Nikkei average closed 7.21 points or 0.04 percent lower at 18,544.45. Its June futures declined 30 to 18,550.
"Short-covering interest in banks and securities firms was strong, but so was profit-taking," said Yasuo Ueki, Nikko Securities general manager.
Turnover was 507 million shares, up from 451 million shares on Monday. Winners beat losers 651 issues to 469. There were 136 issues which were unchanged.
Brokerages were especially well sought after following media reports that Nomura Securities Co Ltd's
president and other directors with voting rights would resign to take responsibility for a recent scandal.

"The recent recovery in trading volume had a positive effect on brokerage shares. Also, the reports (about Nomura) helped to ease psychologically negative factors in the sector," said Keiko Kondo, a strategist at Merrill Lynch Japan Inc.

The buying-back momentum was unaffected by a report late in the afternoon by a local news service that the Finance Ministry is likely to suspend some of Nomura's operations, including stock dealing on its own account, for about three months as a penalty for a scandal linking it with "sokaiya" racketeers. Ministry officials declined to comment on the report and brokers said they were waiting for confirmation.
Nomura ended up 70 yen at 1,370 in turnover of 14.76 million shares, which made it the most heavily traded issue on the first section of the Tokyo bourse.

Bank shares were driven up in the morning by foreign investors, but the buying failed to last into the afternoon. "Bank short-covering got a head start on builders and brokerages and the gains are becoming a little harder to hold on to," said Masayuki Matsumoto, a Dai-Ichi Securities analyst.
"But the buy-back phase is still far from over."

Sumitomo Bank Ltd [8318.T] fell 10 yen to 1,480. Fuji Bank Ltd [8317.T] lost 40 yen to 1,460. Matsumoto added fresh buying of shares in bad-loan laden sectors will not emerge until corporate earnings are announced in May and evidence their financial problems are being dealt with is revealed.
Long-distance telephone service provider DDI Corp
fell 49,000 yen to 790,000 after a downgrade by a foreign securities house.

Nissin Food Products Co Ltd added 250 yen to 2,890 on share repurchase plans, brokers said. On a sector basis, securities firms, food, fisheries, insurance and transport equipment headed the group of advancers. The decliners were led by communications, gas and oil, ship building and land transport.
Brokers said buying by pension funds was seen supporting the indices in times of weakness in coming sessions and fears of a slide were retreating.

"The Nikkei 225 has surpassed the 25-day and the 75-day moving averages but the 100-day average is a very strong barrier to overcome," a dealer at a second-tier brokerage said. The 100-day average stood at 18,867.61 on Tuesday.

In other indices, the TOPIX index gained 0.88 point or 0.06 percent to end at 1,405.58. The Nikkei 300 shed 0.24 point or 0.09 percent to 271.88. The second section index rose 22.55 points or 1.40 percent to 1,631.82.
Turnover was 10.86 million shares, little changed from
Monday.
The over-the-counter index was 11.09 points or 0.99 percent higher at 1,131.99 in late Tokyo.
-- Masako Iijima, Tokyo Equities Desk +81-3-3432-9052 (c) Reuters Limited 1997
